case.title: The Red Water Sample
case.hook: Hi! I’m Sam Park, an engineer. I design and build tools, and I’m your guide for the next few weeks. Today my tools have a real job. A lifeguard at Palmetto Beach brought me a jar of strange-looking water. Let’s find out what’s in it.

notice.head: Water sample · Palmetto Field Lab
notice.title: Sample 18-A: Palmetto Beach, Gulf side
rows: Dead fish on the sand. Swimmers coughing, sneezing, eyes stinging.
notice.line: Sam’s job: find out what is in the water.

stills.alt: Looking down at a Florida beach from the air: waves roll in, and the water near the shore is a muddy red-brown.

case.stillsCredit: Red tide along the Florida coast, 2005: CDC / Lorraine Backer, PhD (CDC Public Health Image Library, public domain). Palmetto Beach, the lifeguard and the sample are made up for this lesson.
case.question: What is hiding in the water at Palmetto Beach, and which tool can find it?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Your eyes see only red-brown water. The cause is a cell so small that two or three side by side are about as wide as one hair.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: how small can each tool go?
clues.t: A red tide cell is too small for your eyes or a hand lens. You need a microscope.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: pick the right tool
clues.t: To COUNT living red tide cells, use a light microscope. An electron microscope shows more detail, but only on dried samples, so nothing on them is alive.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: count the cells
clues.t: Sam counted 12 cells in the square: about 1,200,000 red tide cells in one liter. The FWC chart says that’s HIGH: fish die, people cough, and the water changes color.

solve.title: What is in the water?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Nothing is in the water. The fish died because the water got cold.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 4. What did Sam find in the drop?

options.t: Red tide cells, found with an electron microscope while they were swimming.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Can an electron microscope look at living, swimming cells?

options.t: Red tide: tiny living cells, too small to see. A light microscope found and counted them, and the level is HIGH.
options.why: Case cracked! You picked the right tool and found the cause. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

zoom.title: Sam’s zoom machine
todo: Each stop on the dial is a stronger tool. Tap the new detail at each stop, then turn the dial.

stops.alt: A Florida beach from the air during a red tide. The water near the shore is red-brown.
stops.ask: This is what your eyes see at a red tide beach. Tap the strange color.
stops.hint: Look at the water near the shore. What color is it?
stops.see: Your eyes can see the color. But they can’t see what is making it.

stops.alt: Sand grains up close: green, tan and clear grains of many shapes.
stops.ask: A hand lens on sand from a beach. Tap a grain that looks like glass.
stops.hint: Look for a grain you can almost see through.
stops.see: With a hand lens, each grain has its own shape and color. But red tide cells are still too small to see at 10x.

stops.alt: A circle of light through a microscope eyepiece: a green leaf made of rows of tiny box shapes.
stops.ask: A water plant’s leaf through a light microscope. Tap the tiny shapes that build the leaf.
stops.hint: Look inside the bright circle. Do you see little boxes in rows?
stops.see: A light microscope shows cells, and they can stay alive. Red tide cells are about this size.

stops.alt: A gray, bumpy, three-dimensional cell with a groove around its middle and a curly, whip-like tail.
stops.ask: This is ONE red tide cell. Tap the part that helps it swim.
stops.hint: Look for something curly, like a tiny whip.
stops.see: The tail helps it swim. Two or three of these cells side by side are about as wide as one hair. This cell had to be dried first, so it was not alive.

mitsort.title: How small can each tool go?
todo: Drag each card onto the weakest tool that shows it clearly (or tap a card, then a shelf).

why.t: Scientists start simple. If your eyes can do the job, you don’t need a microscope.

cards.t: A dead fish on the sand
cards.why: A whole fish is big enough to see with just your eyes.
cards.miss: A whole fish is big! Do you need a tool at all?

cards.why: You can see the color from the beach, with no tool.
cards.miss: You can see a color in the sea from the beach. Do you need a tool?

cards.alt: A honey bee wing up close
cards.t: The veins on a bee’s wing
cards.why: Wing veins are thin, but a hand lens shows them easily.
cards.miss: Your eyes see the wing, but not the thin veins clearly. Do you need a whole microscope, or something smaller?

cards.why: Your eyes see some lines. A hand lens shows every ridge and swirl.
cards.miss: Your eyes see some lines, but not every ridge. Which small, quick tool fits?

cards.alt: Tiny glassy living things through a microscope
cards.t: Tiny living things in a drop of seawater
cards.why: Much too small for a hand lens. A light microscope shows them alive.
cards.miss: Too small for a hand lens. And you want to see them alive. Which microscope uses light?

cards.t: Red tide cells swimming in a drop
cards.why: Each cell is thinner than a hair. A light microscope shows them alive and swimming.
cards.miss: Too small for a hand lens. And they are swimming, so they are alive. Which microscope can show living things?

cards.alt: Many grains of pollen with spikes and bumps, colored pink, green and yellow
cards.t: The spikes on one grain of pollen
cards.why: The spikes are tiny, even on a tiny grain. An electron microscope shows them. (The pollen is dried first.)
cards.miss: A light microscope shows the grains, but not the tiny spikes clearly. Which tool sees the smallest bumps?

cards.t: A virus (much smaller than a cell)
cards.why: Most viruses are too small for a light microscope. An electron microscope shows them.
cards.miss: A light microscope can’t see most viruses. Which tool goes even smaller?

bench.title: Pick the right tool
todo: Read each lab request. Think: how small is it, and what does the question ask?
Drag a tool onto the request (or tap a tool, then the request).

why.q: Why can’t the electron microscope do every job?
why.t: It shows the smallest details. But the sample has to be dried and coated first, so nothing on it can be alive.

jobs.alt: A honey bee wing up close
jobs.t: At a beach picnic, look at the veins on a bee’s wing.
jobs.why: Quick, no batteries, and strong enough for wing veins.

miss.light: A light microscope needs a thin slide and a lab. You’re at a picnic!
miss.em: Way too much, and it needs a lab and a dried sample. Pick something you can carry.

jobs.t: Count how many LIVING red tide cells are in one drop of this water.
jobs.why: Strong enough to see each cell, and the cells stay alive in the drop.

miss.lens: Too weak. At 10x, red tide cells are still too small to see.
miss.em: It can’t look at living things. The sample must be dried first, so the cells would be dead.

jobs.alt: A green leaf made of rows of tiny cells
jobs.t: See the cells inside a water plant’s leaf.
jobs.why: Cells are too small for a hand lens, but a light microscope shows them clearly.

miss.lens: Cells are far too small for a hand lens.
miss.em: Too much! A light microscope already shows the cells clearly.

jobs.alt: One bumpy red tide cell with a groove and a whip-like tail
jobs.t: See the tiny groove and the whip-like tail on the outside of ONE red tide cell.
jobs.why: Only an electron microscope shows surface details this small. This real photo was taken with one.

miss.lens: Way too weak for one cell’s outside.
miss.light: A light microscope shows the cell, but not the tiny bumps and grooves on its outside.

bench.q: What makes a tool the RIGHT tool?

opts.miss: Look at request 2. The most powerful tool couldn’t count living cells.

opts.t: The one that fits the question
The one that’s easiest to carry
opts.miss: Look at request 4. A hand lens is easy to carry, but could it do that job?

scope.title: Count the cells
todo: Follow the four steps. The view is a model of what Sam sees.
Then fill in Sam’s lab report.

why.t: A microscope has two lenses. The eyepiece makes things look 10 times bigger. The objective lens makes them 40 times bigger. 10 × 40 = 400.

steps: Count the cells in the square
scope.slideBtn: 🧫 Put the slide on the stage

lines.low: At 40x in all, red tide cells are just specks. Too small to count.
lines.mid: At 100x, you can see tiny golden dots. Still too small to count well. Try the strongest lens.
lines.needLens: These cells are too small to count at this power. Turn to the 40x lens.
lines.needFocus: It’s too blurry to count. Turn the focus knob first.
lines.doneT: Now fill in the lab report below.
lines.fieldAlt: A model of the view through the microscope: a circle of light with small golden red tide cells, a few long striped diatoms, and a dashed counting square.

rule.head: Sam’s rule
rule.t: The count square holds only a tiny bit of one drop. Each cell you counted stands for 100,000 cells in one liter of seawater (about one big water bottle).

tool.name: Hand lens
tool.teaser: Find where a 2x, a 5x and a 10x lens get sharp, then hunt for hidden details.
tool.done: You focused a hand lens like a scientist. A hand lens sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A curved piece of glass in a frame. The curve bends light, so things look bigger. Scientists carry one outdoors because it needs no batteries.

handlens.title: Where does each lens get sharp?
todo: Drag the lens over the photo. Pick 2x, 5x or 10x.
Slide the lens closer or farther until the view is sharp.
Find two hidden details on each thing. Put the lens on one and tap Log what I see.

details.t: Veins that make little window shapes

q.q: The stronger the lens, the ___ you hold it to the thing you’re looking at.

opts.why: Right! The 10x lens got sharp about 2.5 cm away, and the 2x lens about 12 cm away. A stronger lens has more curved glass, so it focuses closer.
Look at your list. Where did 10x get sharp? Where did 2x?
Look at your list. Did every lens get sharp at the same distance?

welcome.label: Welcome · meet Sam
welcome.script: Hi! I’m Sam Park. I’m an engineer, which means I design and build tools to solve problems. I’ll be your guide for the next few weeks. And today, my tools have a real job. Something is wrong at Palmetto Beach. There are dead fish on the sand, and swimmers are coughing. A lifeguard brought me a jar of that water. Let’s find out what’s hiding in it.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · the beach alert and the zoom machine (Clue 1)
warmup.script: First, play the beach alert and tap the three things people noticed. Then try my zoom machine! Each stop on the dial is a stronger tool. Find the new detail at each stop, and keep turning. The last stop is a big surprise.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Hold up a magnifying glass (or a clear glass of water) for “magnify”; cover one eye with your hand for “limitation”.

part1.label: Part 1 · how small can each tool go? (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s an engineer’s rule: start with the simplest tool that works. Drag each card onto the weakest tool that shows it clearly. Your eyes, a hand lens, a light microscope or an electron microscope. Where do you think a red tide cell goes?

part3.label: Part 3 · pick the right tool (Clue 3)
part3.script: My lab got four requests this morning. Read each one carefully. How small is the thing, and what does the question ask you to do? Then drag the right tool onto it. Careful: the most powerful tool can’t do every job.

explore.label: Part 4 · count the cells (Clue 4)
explore.script: Okay, back to the sample! Put the slide on my microscope, turn to the strongest lens, and focus slowly until the cells look sharp. Then count every cell inside the square. When you’re done, we’ll fill in my lab report and check it against the real chart Florida scientists use.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what was hiding in the water, and which tool found it? Then answer two questions, describe three views of one small thing in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says you should always use the most powerful tool you can find. Hmm. Think about the bee wing at the picnic. Then think about counting living red tide cells. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 18.02 (telescopes: tools for things very far away).
closing.script: Case closed! You found red tide hiding in the water, and you picked the right tool for every job. That’s real engineering thinking: the best tool is the one that fits the question. Next time, we flip it around. How do we see things that are really far away, like the Moon and the planets?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how tools help us see things too small for our eyes?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A light microscope can count living red tide cells in a drop of seawater.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “light microscope”, “living” and “red tide cells”. Those words tell which tool fits the job. Small words like “a” and “of” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
